topic: Day 1 · Renal Physiology & the Mechanisms of AKI
speakerBio: Nephrologist and physiologist who teaches the 'two arterioles' model of the kidney and insists that most AKI is a haemodynamics problem hiding in the drug chart.
lectureHTML:
🎯 The case on the table

An 81-year-old woman is admitted with a chest infection. She is on ramipril for hypertension and, because her knees ache, she has been buying ibuprofen over the counter for a fortnight. On the ward she becomes hypotensive with a systolic of 92, the nurse notes she has passed 15 mL of dark urine in four hours, and the morning bloods show a creatinine that has jumped from a baseline of 70 to 210 µmol/L. The FY1 wants to know what has "damaged the kidney." Here is the uncomfortable truth: at this moment nothing is structurally damaged. Her glomeruli are intact. What has collapsed is the physiology that holds glomerular filtration constant — and three of her drugs and one of her vital signs are all pulling on the same set of arterioles. This session is about the machinery, because if you understand how a glomerulus defends its own filtration you can predict, prevent and reverse most of the AKI you will ever see.

1 · 🧠 The master mental model — pre-renal, intrinsic, post-renal

Before a single number, every clinician facing a rising creatinine runs the same triage in their head. It is the most important framework in nephrology because it maps directly onto what you can do about it:

CategoryWhere the problem isOne-line essenceReversibility
Pre-renalBlood getting to the kidneyKidney is starved, not sickFully reversible if caught early
Intrinsic (renal)The kidney tissue itself (tubules, glomeruli, interstitium, vessels)Kidney is structurally injuredDepends on cause & time
Post-renalUrine getting out of the kidneyPlumbing is blockedReversible if relieved before back-pressure injures

The whole of AKI teaching hangs off this fork. Pre-renal and post-renal are functional and reversible — the parenchyma is innocent until proven guilty. But both, if left, march into intrinsic injury: sustained hypoperfusion becomes ischaemic acute tubular necrosis (ATN); sustained obstruction becomes obstructive nephropathy. Time converts the reversible into the structural. That is why AKI is an emergency of minutes-to-hours triage, not a lab curiosity to review on the post-take round.

Pre-renal, intrinsic, post-renal — starving, sick, or blocked. Ask that question first, every time, before you reach for a single biomarker.
💡 The two-second bedside version

"Is the kidney getting enough blood (pre-renal), is the tissue itself injured (intrinsic), or can the urine not get out (post-renal)?" Answer those three and you have already stratified the differential, chosen your first investigation (fluids vs urine microscopy vs bladder scan), and identified whether you are in reversible or structural territory.

2 · ⚙️ What actually sets the GFR — the four Starling determinants

Glomerular filtration is not magic; it is Starling forces across a capillary, and only four things move it. Filtration is driven by the net ultrafiltration pressure and the permeability of the barrier:

GFR = Kf × (PGC − PBS − πGC)
  • Kf — the filtration coefficient (surface area × permeability of the glomerular barrier). Falls in glomerulonephritis, or acutely with mesangial contraction.
  • PGC — hydrostatic pressure inside the glomerular capillary. This is the big lever, and it is set by the balance of afferent and efferent arteriolar tone.
  • PBS — hydrostatic pressure in Bowman's space. Rises when the tubule downstream is obstructed — the mechanism of post-renal AKI.
  • πGC — oncotic pressure of plasma proteins in the capillary, opposing filtration.

Notice what this equation predicts. Obstruction raises PBS and drops GFR with a perfectly normal blood supply — post-renal AKI explained by one term. And the dominant physiological control, PGC, is governed almost entirely by the relative tone of the two arterioles guarding the glomerulus. Learn those two arterioles and you own functional AKI.

3 · 🔧 Glomerular autoregulation — the afferent/efferent double tap

The glomerulus is unique: it sits between two resistance vessels, an afferent arteriole feeding it and an efferent arteriole draining it. Think of a garden hose bulging in the middle — the pressure in the bulge (PGC) depends on how open the inflow tap and how pinched the outflow tap are:

ManoeuvreEffect on PGCEffect on GFREffect on renal blood flow
Constrict AFFERENT (inflow tap)↓↓↓
Dilate AFFERENT↑↑↑
Constrict EFFERENT (outflow tap)↑↑ (up to a point)↓
Dilate EFFERENT↓↓↑

The kidney's job across a wide range of mean arterial pressures (roughly 80–180 mmHg) is to keep PGC, and therefore GFR, almost flat. It does this with two mechanisms working on the afferent arteriole plus a hormonal grip on the efferent:

🩸 The myogenic reflex — the afferent's stretch response

When systemic pressure rises, the afferent arteriole wall is stretched; stretch-activated channels depolarise the smooth muscle and it constricts, protecting the delicate glomerulus from the pressure surge. When pressure falls, it relaxes and dilates to preserve flow. Fast (seconds), reflexive, and the first line of defence.

🔁 Tubuloglomerular feedback (TGF) — the macula densa's report card

Each nephron's own distal tubule loops back to touch its parent glomerulus at the juxtaglomerular apparatus. Specialised cells there, the macula densa, sense the chloride concentration of the fluid arriving in the distal tubule via the NKCC2 cotransporter:

  • If GFR is too high, more NaCl reaches the macula densa → it releases adenosine (and ATP) → the afferent arteriole constricts, dialling GFR back down.
  • If GFR is too low, less NaCl arrives → afferent dilates and renin is released → GFR is defended.

TGF is the negative-feedback thermostat of the single nephron: it couples tubular flow back to filtration so the kidney never floods its own tubules or dries them out.

🧪 The efferent grip — angiotensin II

The hormonal partner works chiefly on the efferent arteriole. Angiotensin II preferentially constricts the efferent arteriole, raising PGC and defending GFR precisely when perfusion pressure is low — the physiological rescue system of the underfilled kidney.

🎯 The two knobs, memorised

Afferent = the INFLOW tap, controlled by myogenic reflex + TGF + prostaglandins (dilators). Efferent = the OUTFLOW tap, controlled by angiotensin II (constrictor). Almost every drug that causes functional AKI works by loosening one of these two grips. Hold this picture and the next section writes itself.

4 · 💊 How everyday drugs cause functional AKI — NSAIDs and ACEi/ARB

Here is where the machinery becomes bedside medicine. When perfusion pressure falls, the kidney leans on two compensations at once: prostaglandins dilate the afferent arteriole (keep the inflow open) and angiotensin II constricts the efferent arteriole (pinch the outflow). Both raise PGC and hold GFR up. Now knock out either one:

Drug classMolecular actionArteriole affectedNet effect on GFR
NSAIDsBlock COX → ↓ prostaglandinsAfferent constricts (loses its dilator)↓ inflow → ↓ PGC → ↓ GFR
ACEi / ARBBlock angiotensin II effectEfferent dilates (loses its constrictor)↓ outflow resistance → ↓ PGC → ↓ GFR

NSAIDs choke the inflow; ACEi/ARBs open the outflow. Either alone drops PGC. In a euvolaemic person with good perfusion, autoregulation has spare capacity and nothing happens — which is why millions take these drugs safely. But in a patient whose kidney is already leaning on both compensations to survive — the hypovolaemic, the septic, the elderly with renovascular disease — removing them causes filtration to fall off a cliff. This is haemodynamic (functional) AKI: the creatinine rises, the parenchyma is untouched, and stopping the drug reverses it within days.

⚠️ The triple whammy

The most dangerous prescription in general medicine is the combination of an ACEi/ARB + a diuretic + an NSAID. The diuretic depletes volume (making the kidney dependent on autoregulation), the NSAID constricts the afferent (kills the inflow compensation), and the ACEi/ARB dilates the efferent (kills the outflow compensation). Every one of the kidney's defences is disabled simultaneously. Add an intercurrent illness with poor oral intake and you have manufactured a textbook AKI. This exact combination is a recognised, preventable, audited cause of hospital admission — always screen the drug chart for it.

NSAIDs squeeze the afferent, ACEi/ARBs relax the efferent — both drop the filtration pressure. Safe in the well-perfused kidney, catastrophic in the underfilled one.

This also explains a classic clue: after starting an ACEi, a creatinine rise of up to ~30% is expected and acceptable — it reflects the intended efferent dilation. A rise beyond that, or an abrupt jump, suggests the patient was critically dependent on angiotensin II to perfuse the glomerulus, which flags bilateral renal artery stenosis — where the whole kidney downstream of a stenosis survives only by maximal efferent constriction.

5 · 🫁 Renal oxygenation — why the outer medulla lives on the edge

The kidney receives ~20–25% of cardiac output, so you would think it is drowning in oxygen. It is not. Regional oxygenation is wildly uneven, and one zone lives permanently on the brink of hypoxia: the outer medulla, home of the S3 segment of the proximal tubule and the medullary thick ascending limb.

Two features conspire against it:

  • Countercurrent oxygen shunting. The vasa recta run as tight hairpin loops; oxygen diffuses directly from the descending to the ascending limb, short-circuiting the deep medulla. The same countercurrent geometry that concentrates urine strips oxygen before it ever reaches the depths.
  • The highest oxygen demand in the kidney. The medullary thick ascending limb runs the NKCC2 pump at ferocious ATP cost to build the concentrating gradient. Oxygen supply is lowest exactly where consumption is highest.

The result: the outer-medullary S3 segment sits at a tissue pO₂ far lower than the cortex, so any drop in perfusion, any nephrotoxin, any surge in reabsorptive workload tips it into ischaemia first. This is why the S3 segment is the signature site of ischaemic and toxic ATN — the anatomy has pre-selected the victim.

💡 The vulnerable zone

The outer medulla is the kidney's watershed. Highest oxygen extraction, lowest oxygen supply, running the most expensive pump in the nephron. When a patient becomes hypotensive, the S3 segment of the proximal tubule and the medullary thick ascending limb are the cells that die first — the cellular link between "pre-renal" hypoperfusion and "intrinsic" ATN.

6 · 🔗 When pre-renal tips into intrinsic — the continuum

Pre-renal azotaemia and ischaemic ATN are not two diseases; they are two points on one timeline. A hypoperfused kidney first defends filtration with autoregulation (pre-renal, reversible — restore the blood pressure and the creatinine falls within a day). If hypoperfusion is severe or prolonged, the oxygen-starved S3 segment and thick ascending limb begin to die; tubular cells detach, cast off into the lumen, and the injury becomes structural ATN that will not reverse the moment you give fluid — it needs days to weeks to regenerate.

FeaturePre-renal azotaemiaEstablished ATN
Tubular functionIntact — avidly reabsorbing Na⁺ & waterFailed — cannot reabsorb
Urine sodiumLow (kidney hoarding salt)High (kidney leaking salt)
FeNa<1%>2%
Urine osmolalityHigh, concentrated (>500)Isosthenuric (~300)
Response to fluidCreatinine falls promptlyNo prompt response
SedimentBland / hyaline castsMuddy-brown granular casts

The urine chemistry is simply reading the tubule's behaviour: a starved-but-alive tubule clings to sodium (low FeNa, concentrated urine); a dead tubule cannot, so sodium and water pour out. These indices, and their many pitfalls, get a full session of their own — but the mechanism to carry away today is that the tubule's sodium handling tells you whether it is alive.

7 · ❤️ The cardiorenal and hepatorenal axes — a teaser

Everything above assumed the kidney's problem was too little blood. But two of the most feared AKIs happen when the circulation itself is deranged despite an apparently full tank:

  • Cardiorenal syndrome. The failing heart cannot generate forward flow, so the kidney senses underperfusion and activates every salt-retaining reflex — yet the patient is oedematous and congested. Worse, high central venous pressure raises renal venous pressure, which impedes glomerular outflow and drops the trans-renal pressure gradient. In heart failure, venous congestion injures the kidney as much as poor forward flow — a mechanism we will draw out fully in its own session.
  • Hepatorenal syndrome. In advanced cirrhosis, splanchnic vasodilation steals blood into the gut, the effective arterial volume collapses, and the kidney responds with intense angiotensin- and vasopressin-driven renal vasoconstriction — a structurally normal kidney throttled by a systemic vascular catastrophe. Terlipressin, albumin and the underlying physiology get a dedicated deep dive.
🎯 The unifying idea

The kidney does not measure your blood volume — it measures the effective arterial blood volume it can sense at the afferent arteriole and baroreceptors. Heart failure and cirrhosis both fool it into behaving as if it were haemorrhaging, even while the patient is overloaded with fluid. Hold that idea; it is the key that unlocks the two hardest AKIs in medicine.

☠️ M&M — the knee that stopped the kidney

A 74-year-old man with well-controlled hypertension on ramipril and bendroflumethiazide developed a painful knee before a weekend away. His GP added regular naproxen and, because he felt "fluey," he ate and drank little for three days. He presented on the Monday confused, with a supine blood pressure of 96/54, a creatinine of 380 (baseline 95), a potassium of 6.4 and no obvious source of sepsis. The admitting team hunted for glomerulonephritis and sent a vasculitis screen. The real diagnosis was mechanical and mundane: a triple whammy (ACEi + thiazide + NSAID) on a volume-depleted elderly kidney had abolished every arm of autoregulation — the NSAID constricted the afferent, the ACEi dilated the efferent, the thiazide emptied the tank. Lessons: the drug chart was the diagnosis; the fix was to stop all three nephrotoxic/hypotensive agents, treat the hyperkalaemia, and rehydrate — the creatinine halved within 48 hours and normalised in a week, with no immunosuppression and no biopsy. He was harmed not by exotic disease but by three ordinary tablets pulling on the same arterioles. Always reconcile the drug chart before you order the vasculitis screen.

8 · 🎯 Take-home messages

  1. Pre-renal, intrinsic, post-renal — starving, sick, or blocked — is the master triage; run it before any biomarker, because it separates reversible from structural and dictates your first move.
  2. GFR = Kf × (PGC − PBS − πGC). PGC is the dominant lever and is set by afferent vs efferent tone; a rise in PBS is the entire mechanism of obstruction.
  3. Autoregulation keeps GFR flat across MAP 80–180 mmHg via the fast myogenic reflex and tubuloglomerular feedback on the afferent, plus angiotensin II gripping the efferent.
  4. NSAIDs constrict the afferent (loss of prostaglandin dilation); ACEi/ARBs dilate the efferent (loss of angiotensin II constriction). Both drop filtration pressure — harmless in the well-perfused kidney, catastrophic in the underfilled one. Beware the triple whammy.
  5. The outer medulla / S3 segment is the kidney's hypoxic watershed — highest oxygen demand, lowest supply — and dies first, converting pre-renal hypoperfusion into intrinsic ATN.
  6. The tubule's sodium handling reveals whether it is alive: low FeNa & concentrated urine = starved-but-alive (pre-renal); high FeNa & isosthenuric = dead tubule (ATN).
  7. The kidney senses effective arterial volume, not total body water — the reason heart failure (cardiorenal) and cirrhosis (hepatorenal) injure structurally normal kidneys.

moderatorQs.q: Explain, in mechanistic terms, why an NSAID and an ACE inhibitor cause acute kidney injury by opposite actions on the glomerulus.
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Both drop the glomerular capillary pressure (PGC) that drives filtration, but from opposite ends of the tuft. NSAIDs block cyclo-oxygenase and remove the prostaglandins that dilate the AFFERENT arteriole, so the inflow tap constricts and less blood enters the glomerulus. ACE inhibitors and ARBs remove angiotensin II, which normally constricts the EFFERENT arteriole, so the outflow tap dilates and pressure escapes downstream. NSAIDs choke the inflow; ACEi/ARBs open the outflow — either way PGC falls and GFR drops. In a euvolaemic patient there is spare autoregulatory capacity and nothing happens; in a hypovolaemic, septic or renovascular kidney that is already leaning on both compensations, removing them causes filtration to collapse — a functional, reversible AKI with a structurally normal kidney.

moderatorQs.q: Why is the outer medulla the region of the kidney most vulnerable to ischaemic injury, despite the kidney receiving a quarter of the cardiac output?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Because oxygen supply and demand are catastrophically mismatched there. The vasa recta run as countercurrent hairpin loops, so oxygen diffuses directly from descending to ascending limbs and is shunted away before it reaches the depths — the same geometry that concentrates urine strips the medulla of oxygen. Meanwhile the medullary thick ascending limb and the S3 segment of the proximal tubule run the most ATP-expensive pumps in the nephron to build the concentrating gradient. Lowest supply, highest demand: the outer medulla therefore sits at a baseline tissue pO₂ close to hypoxic, so any fall in perfusion or any nephrotoxin tips the S3 segment into ischaemia first. That anatomy is why ischaemic and toxic ATN both target the outer medulla, and it is the cellular bridge between pre-renal hypoperfusion and intrinsic tubular necrosis.

moderatorQs.q: A patient's creatinine rises by 25% two weeks after starting an ACE inhibitor. Is that acceptable, and when would it worry you?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: A rise of up to about 30% is expected and acceptable — it is the direct, intended consequence of efferent arteriolar dilation lowering PGC, and it does not mean structural injury; you continue the drug and recheck. It worries me when the rise is greater than ~30%, abrupt, or accompanied by a jump in potassium or a fall in urine output, because that says the glomerulus was critically dependent on angiotensin II to maintain filtration pressure. The classic sinister explanation is bilateral renal artery stenosis (or stenosis to a single functioning kidney), where the whole nephron mass survives only by maximal efferent constriction; block angiotensin II and filtration collapses. Volume depletion and concurrent NSAID use are the other precipitants to exclude before attributing it to renovascular disease.

audienceQs.q: What actually is 'tubuloglomerular feedback' and why should I care on the ward?
audienceQs.answerHTML: It is the single nephron's built-in thermostat. Each distal tubule loops back to touch its own glomerulus at the juxtaglomerular apparatus, where the macula densa cells sense the chloride concentration of the fluid arriving via the NKCC2 cotransporter. If GFR is too high, more NaCl reaches them and they release adenosine, constricting the afferent arteriole to dial GFR back down; if GFR is too low, less NaCl arrives, the afferent dilates and renin is released to defend filtration. Why care on the ward? It explains why loop diuretics (which block NKCC2) blind the macula densa, and it is the physiology behind the low urinary sodium of a starved-but-alive pre-renal kidney versus the salt-leaking dead tubule of ATN — the basis of the FeNa you will order.

audienceQs.q: Which combination on a drug chart should make me phone the team about AKI risk?
audienceQs.answerHTML: The 'triple whammy': an ACE inhibitor or ARB + a diuretic + an NSAID, especially in an older patient or anyone with an intercurrent illness and poor oral intake. Mechanistically it disables every arm of glomerular autoregulation at once — the diuretic empties the tank so the kidney becomes autoregulation-dependent, the NSAID constricts the afferent by removing prostaglandins, and the ACEi/ARB dilates the efferent by removing angiotensin II. It is a recognised, audited, preventable cause of hospital admission. When you see it, flag it — advise holding the NSAID and, during acute illness or dehydration, temporarily suspending the ACEi/ARB and diuretic (the 'sick day rules'), and check renal function.

audienceQs.q: How do I quickly tell at the bedside whether a rising creatinine is pre-renal or already established ATN?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Read the tubule's behaviour and its response to volume. A pre-renal (starved but alive) kidney hoards sodium and water: urine sodium is low, urine is concentrated (osmolality >500), the FeNa is <1%, the sediment is bland, and crucially the creatinine falls promptly once you restore perfusion with fluids or by treating the cause. An established ATN tubule is dead and cannot reabsorb: urine sodium is high, urine is isosthenuric (~300 mOsm), FeNa is >2%, you see muddy-brown granular casts, and there is no quick response to fluid — it needs days to weeks to regenerate. Remember the indices are thrown off by diuretics, CKD and sepsis, so the honest bedside test is often a properly assessed fluid challenge plus a fresh look at the urine under the microscope.
